De las potencias de aritmética sabes que: From the powers of arithmetic you know that $2^3 = 8$ and that multiplying powers with the same base adds the exponents. From quadratic equations, that a change of variable turns a new problem into a familiar one. Here the unknown climbs up into the exponent, and getting it down from there needs a new operation, the logarithm, whose properties are those of powers read backwards.
Hasta ahora la incógnita siempre estaba: Until now the unknown was always in the base: $x^2$, $3x$. And if it is in the exponent? $2^x = 8$ can be solved by eye ($x=3$), but $2^x = 10$ cannot. A new operation is needed to undo the exponential: the logarithm.
En palabras: <em>el logaritmo en base $a: In words: the logarithm to base $a$ of $b$ is the exponent to which $a$ must be raised to get $b$. It is literally “the missing exponent”.
Eso es $81 : 3$. El logaritmo no divide:: That is $81 : 3$. The logarithm does not divide: it asks which exponent the 3 has to be raised to.
$3^3 = 27$, no 81. Hace falta una potenc: $3^3 = 27$, not 81. One more power is needed.
Dos bases tienen nombre propio: $\\log x: Two bases have names of their own: $\log x$ (with no base) means base 10, and $\ln x$ is the natural logarithm, to base $e \approx 2{.}71828$. In higher mathematics “log” almost always means “ln”.
John Napier publicó las primeras tablas: John Napier published the first tables of logarithms in 1614 with a purely practical aim: turning multiplications into additions, which are far quicker to do by hand. For astronomers it was a revolution; it is said to have “doubled the life of the astronomer”. Out of it came the slide rule, which took people to the Moon and did not retire until pocket calculators arrived, in the nineteen-seventies.

La tercera es la más útil de todas: <str: The third is the most useful of all: it brings the exponent down, and that is exactly what we need to isolate an unknown that sits up there.

El logaritmo <strong>no</strong> reparte: The logarithm does not distribute over sums: $\log(x+y) \ne \log x + \log y$. What it turns into sums is products, not sums into anything.
El producto se convierte en suma, y el e: The product turns into a sum, and the exponent 2 comes down multiplying only $\log y$.
The square affects only $y$, not $x$. That would be the expansion of $\log(xy)^2$.
El producto de dentro se convierte en <e: The product inside turns into a sum of logarithms, not a product.
La propiedad de que el logaritmo convier: The property that logarithms turn products into sums changed the history of science: for three hundred years, astronomers and navigators multiplied enormous numbers by looking them up in tables of logarithms, adding and undoing, because adding is vastly quicker than multiplying by hand. The slide rule, which took people to the Moon, was no more than two logarithms sliding over one another.
En estas ecuaciones la incógnita está <e: In these equations the unknown is up there, in the exponent, and the usual tools do not reach it: an exponent cannot be isolated by adding or dividing. This is where the third property above earns its keep. There are two routes, and it pays to recognise which one applies before starting to work.
<strong>Si se pueden igualar las bases</: If the bases can be made equal, the exponents are set equal: $2^{x+1} = 8 = 2^3 \Rightarrow x+1 = 3$.
<strong>Si no</strong>, se toman logarit: If not, you take logarithms of both sides and bring the exponent down.

<strong>Ver la estructura.</strong> $3^{: See the structure. $3^{2x} = (3^x)^2$. The equation is “something squared, minus 4 times that something, plus 3”: quadratic in $3^x$.

<strong>Cambiar.</strong> Con $t = 3^x$: Change. With $t = 3^x$ you are left with $t^2 - 4t + 3 = 0$, whose solutions are $t = 1$ and $t = 3$ (they add to 4 and multiply to 3).
<strong>Deshacer el cambio.</strong> $t$: Undo the change. $t$ is not the answer; $x$ is. $3^x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 0$, and $3^x = 3 \Rightarrow x = 1$.
$t = 1$ y $t = 3$. ¿Es eso la solución?: $t = 1$ and $t = 3$. Is that the solution? What is missing?
Si una de las $t$ hubiera salido negativ: If one of the $t$ had come out negative, it would be discarded: $3^x$ is always positive and there is no $x$ with $3^x = -2$.

En las ecuaciones logarítmicas es <stron: In logarithmic equations it is compulsory to check the solutions at the end: the logarithm exists only for positive numbers, so a solution can come out algebraically correct but impossible. It is discarded.

$\\log(-3)$ no existe. En las logarítmic: $\log(-3)$ does not exist. In logarithmic equations the check is part of the solution.
Una potencia de base positiva nunca vale: A power with a positive base is never 0 and never negative. The equation has no solution.
Estas ecuaciones responden a «¿cuánto ti: These equations answer “how long does it take?”. How long an investment takes to double, how long a drug takes to fall by half in the blood — the half-life printed on the leaflet — how old a bone is from the carbon 14 left in it. In all three the result is known and the exponent is wanted, and isolating an exponent is exactly what the logarithm was invented for.
Hay un uso de los logaritmos que se ve c: There is one use of logarithms that is seen constantly in graphs and is worth recognising. If two quantities are related by a power, $y = c\,x^{-\alpha}$, taking logarithms leaves $\log y = \log c - \alpha \log x$: a straight line. So, by drawing both axes on a logarithmic scale, a power law is recognised at a glance because the points fall in line, and the gradient is the exponent. That is how the so-called scaling laws of language models are presented, in [[ia-llm|the topic on LLMs]].
